2017 · CVPR 2017 · Benchmarks & Evals

Are You Smarter Than A Sixth Grader? Textbook Question Answering for Multimodal Machine Comprehension

TQA pulls 1,076 lessons straight out of middle-school science textbooks — text, diagrams, images, vocabulary and all — and pairs them with 26,260 questions that can only be answered from that lesson's own content. It's a deliberately harder, more bounded cousin of VQA and SQuAD: 2017's best attention and memory-network models land almost exactly at random on True/False, and clear it by only about ten points on text Multiple Choice and six on diagram Multiple Choice.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By 2017, "machine comprehension" (MC) and "visual question answering" (VQA) had each raced ahead on their own turf — MC on datasets like SQuAD, where the knowledge is a short block of text, and VQA on datasets built from Microsoft COCO images (VQA, COCO-QA, FM-IQA, Visual Madlibs), where the knowledge is a single photograph. The paper's core complaint about that split is architectural: in both lines of work, "the context is usually about a single modality (either language or vision)." Real-world knowledge doesn't come pre-sorted that way — it's, in the paper's phrase, "spread across text documents, images and videos", and a system that can only read or only see is answering a narrower question than the one it claims to.

VQA specifically has a second problem the paper calls out directly, using the VQA dataset's own example: the question "Does this person have 20/20 vision?" requires detecting eyeglasses and applying outside common sense (people with 20/20 vision don't usually wear them) — knowledge that has to come from somewhere other than the supplied image, and in practice comes from whatever correlations a model picks up from the training split. That makes the knowledge VQA systems need "unbounded," and the paper argues it's a confound: you can't cleanly tell whether a model is reading the image or has memorized a shortcut from training data.

The paper's fix is a new task it names Multi-Modal Machine Comprehension (M3C): read a multi-modal context (text and diagrams and images together) and answer a question using only that context, the same read-then-answer contract MC already uses for text, just extended to more modalities. Because the knowledge is "bounded to the multi-modal context supplied with the question", M3C is pitched as easier to evaluate honestly than VQA's open-ended common-sense setting, while still forcing genuinely multi-modal reasoning that single-modality MC can't test. Textbook Question Answering (TQA) is the testbed built to instantiate M3C at real complexity: the diagrams and text of a middle-school science curriculum, chosen because — in the paper's words — "the textual and diagrammatic content in middle school science reference fairly complex phenomena that occur in the world", making it "a good test bed for the M3C paradigm."

// how it works

The dataset, and the baselines built to fail on it

TQA is built from 1,076 lessons spanning Life Science, Earth Science and Physical Science, downloaded from the CK-12 curriculum website (ck12.org) in August 2016. Each lesson bundles several things together: paragraphs of lesson text, diagrams and natural images, a Vocabulary section defining the lesson's scientific terms, and a Lesson Summary (typically five sentences). Across all 1,076 lessons that's 78,338 sentences and 3,455 images. Lessons also link to 2,156 instructional videos — explicitly not part of the dataset itself, offered only "to encourage future research in extracting content from instructional videos."

The authors noticed a gap during construction: lesson text and image captions didn't always cover what a diagram showed, on the theory that a teacher normally fills that gap live in class. To patch it inside the dataset, they added a small set (typically three to five per lesson) of Instructional Diagrams — to the lessons that already had diagram questions, not to every lesson — with crowd-sourced rich captions describing the scientific concepts each diagram illustrates.

Questions. Each lesson carries multiple-choice questions, with between two and seven answer choices. TQA totals 26,260 questions, of which 12,567 come with an accompanying diagram (the paper's "diagram questions"); the remaining questions have no diagram ("text questions"). Most questions are drawn straight from CK-12's own Workbooks and Quizzes; the paper doesn't separately describe how those questions' wrong-answer choices were authored, so they are presumably the textbook publisher's own multiple-choice distractors rather than a distinct annotation step. Diagram questions were comparatively scarce in that source material, so the authors supplemented them: they pulled a list of scientific topics per lesson, queried Google Image Search, manually filtered the results down to images matching the lesson's content, and ended up with 2,749 diagrams spread across 85 lessons. Crowd workers (via MightyAI) were then shown the full lesson plus one of these diagrams and asked to "write down a middle school science question that required the diagram to answer it correctly, and was answerable using the provided lesson" — that crowd-sourcing step is where the diagram-question multiple-choice options for this supplemental set come from; the paper does not describe a separate distractor-authoring step beyond this instruction.

Splits are made at the lesson level, not the question level, specifically so that no lesson's content leaks across train/val/test: 666 lessons / 15,154 questions train, 200 lessons / 5,309 questions validation, 210 lessons / 5,797 questions test. Because some lessons cover overlapping concepts, the authors grouped concept-overlapping lessons together before splitting, "to minimize the concept overlap between data splits."

Four 2017-era baselines

Section 5 adapts four existing architectures to TQA rather than proposing a new one — the point of the paper is to show the gap, not close it. The Text Only model extends Memory Networks: since a full lesson (often 1,000+ words) won't fit in GPU memory as a single batch, it first retrieves the single most relevant paragraph by tf-idf overlap with the question, then LSTM-encodes that paragraph, the question, and each answer choice. An attention mechanism scores each paragraph word against the question:

Stj = M′⊤:t U′:j // similarity between the t-th paragraph word and j-th question word (both LSTM outputs); a = softmax(maxcol S) attends over the paragraph, m = Σt aₜM′:t is the resulting "predicted answer" vector, compared against each choice's summed embedding to pick a softmax winner.

Two variants extend this to diagrams: Text + Image pushes the diagram/image through an ImageNet-pretrained VGG network and adds its 7×7 grid of 512-D last-conv-layer patch vectors into the same memory as the text (a standard VQA-style attention setup, per the paper "similar to popular models employed in the VQA paradigm"). Text + DPG instead uses Diagram Parse Graphs — structured object/relationship parses from the authors' own earlier AI2D parser (Kembhavi et al., A Diagram Is Worth A Dozen Images, ECCV 2016) — mechanically translated into factual sentences (e.g. a "mouse"–"cat" DPG edge becomes "mouse is connected to cat") and folded into the same paragraph-based pipeline. Finally, BiDAF — at the time ranked second on the SQuAD leaderboard — is adapted from span prediction to multiple choice by comparing its predicted answer span against each choice and picking the closest match.

// what they found

Near-random on True/False, a real gap on Multiple Choice

Table 1 reports percentage accuracy for all four baselines plus a random-choice baseline, broken out by question type (the paper's table caption gives no split — train/val/test — for these numbers, and none is stated in the Section 5 text either); note that Text+Image and Text+DPG were only evaluated on Diagram MC — their Text T/F and Text MC cells are marked N/A, not low scores:

ModelInspired byText T/FText MCDiagram MCAll
Random (baseline)N/A50.022.725.028.4
Text OnlyMemory Networks50.232.929.933.8
Text + ImageVQAN/AN/A29.933.8
Text + DPGDSDP-NETN/AN/A31.334.6
BiDAFBiDAF50.432.230.133.7

Two things jump out from that table, and they're separate findings — one is about True/False questions, the other about Multiple Choice, and neither should be read as an "overall" number since "All" mixes both. On Text True/False, only two of the four baselines were even evaluated — Text+Image and Text+DPG have no Text T/F score at all — and both of those two, Text Only and BiDAF, land within half a point of the 50.0% coin-flip floor (50.2%, 50.4%): the paper attributes this directly to the nature of the T/F questions themselves: "Most T/F questions in this dataset are not simple lookups but require paraphrasing, multiple sentences, reasoning to be answered correctly," which standard attention models "are not good at." On Text Multiple Choice questions — again only Text Only and BiDAF have a score — both do better than random by roughly 10 points: Text Only reaches 32.9% against a 22.7% random floor (+10.2 points), BiDAF reaches 32.2% (+9.5 points); the paper is explicit that this is still a low bar given the number of genuinely complex questions in the set. Diagram MC is a separate, smaller gap — see below.

On Diagram MC — the one question type all four baselines were run on — the gap over random is smaller than on Text MC: the best of the four, Text+DPG at 31.3%, is +6.3 points over the 25.0% floor, against Text MC's +10.2. Adding the raw VGG image patches (Text + Image, 29.9%) gives literally no improvement over ignoring the diagram entirely (Text Only, also 29.9%) — the two numbers are identical. Adding the structured DPG-derived diagram parse instead (Text + DPG, 31.3%) does help, by 1.4 points over Text Only, which the paper notes "is consistent with the findings in Kembhavi et al. in the AI2D dataset" — i.e. structure beats raw pixels for these diagrams in both papers. The authors offer three candidate explanations for the across-the-board weakness: TQA's lesson contexts are much longer than prior MC datasets' (making it hard to fit a whole lesson into an attention memory); folding multiple modalities into one memory is itself an unsolved problem; and many questions require multi-hop reasoning or show large lexical variation from the context, which the era's memory-network architectures — validated mainly on synthetic multi-hop toy tasks like bAbI — were not built to handle at this scale.

Section 4's separate, human-coded analysis backs up why: on a 250-question sample of each type, text questions split fairly evenly between needing a single sentence and needing multiple sentences within a paragraph (roughly 39-40% of the sample each) — only the single-sentence share is directly comparable to SQuAD, where the paper says "a majority of questions can be answered by 1 sentence," so TQA's ~39% single-sentence share is already a harder distribution on that one comparison. For diagram questions that actually require the diagram to answer (a subset of the 250 sampled, per Figure 4(b)/(c)/(d)), "Very few questions can be answered with just a classification of the diagram, and more than 50% need a rich structure to be parsed out of the diagram," while "fewer than 5% of diagrams can be trivially answered by just the raw OCR text" — i.e. among the diagram questions that need the diagram at all, the diagrams are doing real work, not standing in as decoration.

Figure 6 in the paper (reproduced below) walks through eight qualitative categories of questions the authors found interesting during their analysis — rich diagram parsing, questions needing multiple sentences, questions needing both text and diagram, ordering/sequence questions, "N of Above"-style answers, hypothetical questions, analogy questions, and simple-math questions — each shown with its correct answer and the supporting passage.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

TQA's baselines are honest 2017-era comparisons for what they are — Memory Networks, a VQA-style CNN+attention model, the authors' own prior AI2D diagram parser, and a then state-of-the-art SQuAD model (BiDAF, "currently ranks second best on the SQuAD leaderboard") — and the paper is upfront that none of them work: "these models do not perform well on TQA." That candor is a strength of the write-up. But it also means the headline finding is closer to our own extensions of contemporary architectures underperform than no reasonable model can solve this, since no baseline external to the authors' own reimplementations is included; a reader from 2017 has no way to tell from this paper alone whether a better-tuned contemporary system would close much of the gap.

The near-random True/False numbers (50.2% and 50.4%, just above the 50.0% floor — only Text Only and BiDAF have a T/F score) are the paper's most striking result, but the "All" column in Table 1 buries them inside an aggregate that also includes the much-less-random Multiple Choice numbers — a reader skimming only the "All" column (33.7-34.6% vs. 28.4% random) would come away thinking the gap over random is a fairly uniform ~5-6 points everywhere, when it is actually close to zero on T/F and roughly 10 points on Text MC. The paper's own prose does separate these findings correctly in Section 5.4; it's the table's single combined column, read on its own, that would mislead. A related oddity the table doesn't explain: Text+Image and Text+DPG carry no Text T/F or Text MC score, yet both still report an "All" number (33.8%, 34.6%) in the same range as Text Only's and BiDAF's — the paper never states what those two models' "All" figure is aggregated over, given they were never run on text questions at all.

On data provenance: the lesson text, images, vocabulary and workbook/quiz questions all come from CK-12's public middle-school curriculum site, downloaded wholesale in August 2016; a further 2,749 diagrams were pulled separately from Google Image Search across 85 lessons and manually filtered for relevance, a more exposed provenance path since those images were never part of CK-12's own curriculum. The paper describes this sourcing plainly but does not discuss licensing terms, attribution requirements, or copyright status anywhere in the text — a gap that is unremarkable for a 2017 CVPR paper (this kind of scraped-benchmark licensing scrutiny largely postdates it) but is worth flagging for anyone reusing the dataset downstream. Separately, the lesson-level train/val/test split is explicitly designed only against concept overlap between lessons ("care has been taken to group these lessons before splitting the data, so as to minimize the concept overlap between data splits") — a 2017-appropriate notion of leakage. The paper has nothing to say about the modern pretraining-corpus sense of contamination (a public curriculum site being absorbed into a future web-scale training set), since that concern did not yet exist in the field's vocabulary at publication time.

On whether diagram questions need the diagram: the paper's own Section 4.3 analysis is the strongest evidence in its favor here — of the diagram questions that actually require the diagram to answer, a human-coded sample found more than 50% "need a rich structure to be parsed out of the diagram" and fewer than 5% "can be trivially answered by just the raw OCR text", i.e. the authors checked this concern themselves, on the relevant sub-population, rather than asserting it of all diagram questions. What the paper does not report is a model-side check of the same question: a text-only or choices-only baseline run specifically on the diagram-question subset to see how far a model can get by exploiting question phrasing or answer-choice patterns alone, independent of any image or diagram content (the closest it gets is the Text Only row of Table 1, which does include the lesson's textual context, not a context-blind control). Given how often later multiple-choice benchmarks turned out to be partly solvable from the choices alone, that specific control's absence is worth naming, even though it wasn't yet standard practice when this paper was written.

baselines

Reasonable state-of-the-art extensions for 2017 (Memory Networks, VQA-style CNN attention, the authors' own AI2D parser, BiDAF), but all four are the authors' own re-implementations/extensions — no independently-published contemporary system is compared, so the size of the true achievable gap over these baselines is untested within the paper.

contamination

Addressed only as lesson-level concept overlap between TQA's own train/val/test splits, which the paper does control for. Not addressed, and not yet a field concern in 2017: whether CK-12's public web content could later leak into pretraining corpora for downstream models.

what's missed

A context-blind (text-only-of-question-and-choices, no lesson, no diagram) control baseline on the diagram-question subset — the paper verifies via human coding that diagrams are usually necessary, but never verifies with a model that the choices alone aren't partly guessable.

would raise confidence

An external, non-author-implemented contemporary baseline; a choices-only ablation per question type; and, given the near-floor Text T/F numbers, some analysis of whether that 50% is single failure mode (e.g. numeric/quantitative reasoning) or many small ones.

// bottom line

TQA is a well-documented, carefully-split resource that does what it sets out to do: force a model to read a genuinely multi-modal, textbook-length context rather than a single sentence or a single photograph, and its own Section 4 analysis backs up that the diagrams and multi-sentence text are doing real work. The 2017 baselines it ships alongside the dataset are appropriately humble about their own failure rather than oversold, which is the paper's best eval instinct — but because every reported model is the authors' own build, and no choices-only control accompanies the diagram-necessity claim, the paper's numbers describe what memory networks and BiDAF-style attention could do with this dataset in 2017, not a tight bound on what the dataset requires.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. TQA pairs 1,076 middle-school science lessons (78,338 sentences, 3,455 images, from CK-12) with 26,260 multiple-choice questions — 12,567 of them tied to a specific diagram — split by lesson (666/200/210 lessons; 15,154/5,309/5,797 questions) to keep concepts from leaking across train/val/test.
  2. Of the four 2017 baselines the authors built — Text Only (Memory Networks), Text+Image (VQA-style), Text+DPG (their own AI2D diagram parser), and BiDAF — only Text Only and BiDAF were evaluated on text questions, and both landed within half a point of the 50.0% random floor on Text True/False (50.2%, 50.4%) and only about 10 points above random on Text Multiple Choice (22.7%→32.9% at best). On Diagram MC, the question type all four were run on, the gap over random is smaller (+6.3 points at best, 31.3% vs. a 25.0% floor): adding raw VGG image features gave zero lift over ignoring the diagram entirely (29.9% either way), while structured diagram parses (DPG) added 1.4 points.
  3. The paper's own human-coded analysis (250 questions per type) found that, of the diagram questions that actually require the diagram, more than half need a "rich structure" parsed out of it and fewer than 5% are answerable from raw OCR text alone — the diagrams are load-bearing, not decorative, for that sub-population by the paper's own accounting, even though no model-side choices-only control tests the same claim.
